title: Signature Magic-Number Detection — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Every format detection starts with magic numbers — the fixed byte sequences formats place at the start of their files. The detector checks these signatures longest-first against the file's head bytes, returning the most specific match. A confidence accompanies each match: exact magic plus sane structure scores higher than magic alone. This is the same mechanism the Unix 'file' command has used for decades, and it remains the most reliable first step in format identification. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
demo:
SIGS = [(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n", "png"), (b"GIF8", "gif"), (b"%PDF", "pdf")]
def detect(head):
    for sig, name in sorted(SIGS, key=lambda s: -len(s[0])):
        if head.startswith(sig): return name
    return "unknown"
print(detect(b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n...."))
print(detect(b"GIF89a...."))

title: Signature Extension Disambiguation — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Extensions are hints, not truth: a '.csv' might be tab-separated, and a '.json' might be JSON lines. The disambiguator weighs the extension against content evidence — delimiters, structural tokens, magic bytes — and content wins ties. When evidence conflicts, it reports both hypotheses with scores instead of picking silently. This careful weighing prevents the classic failure of trusting a renamed file. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
demo:
def disambiguate(ext, head):
    votes = {}
    votes["by-ext"] = ext.lstrip(".")
    votes["by-content"] = "tsv" if b"\t" in head else "csv"
    winner = votes["by-content"]
    print("ext says %s, content says %s -> %s" % (votes["by-ext"], votes["by-content"], winner))
disambiguate(".csv", b"a\tb\n1\t2")

title: Signature Conversion Registry — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Conversions are registered as directed edges between formats — CSV to JSON, JSON to CSV, markdown to text — each with a converter function and a fidelity note. Multi-step conversions compose automatically: if A converts to B and B to C, the engine offers A to C and reports the chain. Lossy steps are flagged so callers know what was sacrificed. A declarative registry keeps conversion logic discoverable instead of scattered through application code. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.

title: Signature Tabular Pivoting — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Tabular data constantly needs reshaping: CSV rows to JSON objects, JSON arrays back to CSV, wide tables to long form. The pivoting engine treats the header row as the schema contract and converts losslessly in both directions, preserving types where the format allows. Malformed rows — wrong column counts, bad quoting — are quarantined with line numbers instead of aborting the conversion. Reliable pivoting is the unglamorous workhorse underneath most data interchange. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
demo:
rows = [["name", "n"], ["a", "1"], ["b", "2"]]
objs = [dict(zip(rows[0], r)) for r in rows[1:]]
back = [[k for k in objs[0]]] + [[o[k] for k in objs[0]] for o in objs]
print("to json:", objs)
print("roundtrip ok:", back == rows)

title: Signature Encoding Detection — Core Method
description: Signature original by Justin Addam Higgins. Text arrives in many encodings, and guessing wrong produces mojibake. The detector checks for byte-order marks first, then tries strict UTF-8 decoding, then falls back to statistical heuristics over single-byte encodings. Every detection reports a confidence, and low-confidence results keep the raw bytes alongside the decoded text. Correct encoding handling is invisible when it works and catastrophic when it does not, which is why it deserves its own engine stage. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method. Lineage: Signature-line counterpart of the public method of the same name, filed as a Signature original in the Signature archive.
